albums.blurb: Hiroshi Suzuki was a Japanese trombonist who left for the U.S. in 1971 to play in Buddy Rich's band; on a 1975 visit home he reunited with his former Freedom Unity bandmates — keyboardist Hiromasa Suzuki, saxophonist Takeru Muraoka, bassist Kunimitsu Inaba, and drummer Akira Ishikawa — for a two-day session at Nippon Columbia's Tokyo studio. The result, released in February 1976, is five unhurried, entirely instrumental trombone-led grooves, and by far his best-known work.
albums.reception: The album sold poorly and passed largely unnoticed in Japan on release, but decades later became one of the most sought-after Japanese jazz records among collectors and the lo-fi beats scene, prompting a remastered reissue from We Release Jazz in June 2021.

albums.blurb: A one-off pairing of two South Londoners: guitarist-producer Tom Misch, following his softer 2018 debut Geography, and drummer Yussef Dayes, previously half of the jazz duo Yussef Kamaal. Released in April 2020 on Misch's Beyond the Groove label and distributed through Blue Note, the album trades Misch's usual polish for darker, looser jams built around Dayes' drumming, with a Freddie Gibbs feature on "Nightrider."
albums.reception: It debuted at number four on the UK Albums Chart — Misch's highest chart placement and Dayes' first chart appearance — and was nominated for Best Album at the 2021 Ivor Novello Awards.

albums.blurb: Japanese Breakfast is the project of Korean-American songwriter Michelle Zauner, whose first two albums were written in the shadow of her mother's death. Jubilee, her third, released on Dead Oceans in June 2021, was conceived as a deliberate turn toward joy, dressing her indie songwriting in strings, horns, and synth-pop arrangements; it arrived the same year as her bestselling memoir Crying in H Mart.
albums.reception: Jubilee earned Japanese Breakfast nominations for Best New Artist and Best Alternative Music Album at the 2022 Grammy Awards.
